comments.author: @Yuenpl
comments.text:
About leaving Tokyo, I work here. During COVID etc., a lot of companies went for remote work, or at least very generous hybrid work (e.g. 1-2 days in the office per week only). That let a lot of people move further away - you don't have to commute so much (or at all), so time-wise can afford to leave further out of Tokyo. With how good train connections are here - sometimes even quite far away. A lot of my friends made the move. 

But, the vast majority of companies have now fully gone back on remote work and now require 4-5 days per week at the office. It's common even in IT, where I work. So people are again stuck in Tokyo.

There's more about how the business in Japan is heavily contributing to a lot of the problems discussed in the video:
- Young people don't have enough money to marry and start families. Especially with recent cost of life increases. Rent in Tokyo is absolutely out of control for what you're getting. Yet, business in Japan sits on absolutely astronomical pile of cash, but doesn't want to raise salaries in any meaningful ways. IF they do it, it barely covers the inflation. Combine this with historically weak yen...
- So much is told and tried about making it easier for working parents - paternal childcare leave, mothers returning to work after maternity leave, etc. In theory it's all in law to support it. In practice most companies are still against it. People who do it will be shunned, will have their opportunities cut, etc. Culturally there's a huge stigma against it. Basically the business culture in Japan is still anti-family. Your first loyalty should still be the company, family only second. 

On top of that there's the same dating crisis as everywhere in the world, people just can't connect, more and more are single even if they try to date, or just give up and remain single. 

So throwing money at the problem is not gonna help, problems are wider and deeper (and sadly - seen across the whole western world).

comments.author: @ChickensAndGardening
comments.text:
Some fun facts: every developed country's population, except for Israel, is shrinking. This includes China, Russia, and even some of the Muslim majority countries like Turkey where birth rates are starting to slow down. The U.S. would be shrinking if not for immigration. 
The reporter mentioned Nagi, where they made a concerted effort starting about 25 years ago to encourage large families, and they have succeeded. They are visited by delegations from all over Japan and from Korea as well. 
Kyoto is a family friendly city and there are a lot of children there.
Okinawa is a more traditional/conservative area where people marry younger and have larger families.
However these places are offset by Tokyo's gigantic size and population of young people choosing to be single and childless, or unable to build a family in an expensive city. 
However, there is a recent trend of young couples relocating out of the big cities to smaller towns that are more affordable; remote work has made this possible. 
Japan doesn't have the "blue state/red state" bitter divisions that the United States suffers from, other than perhaps more conservative attitudes toward women staying at home and raising children versus having their own careers.
I have visited Japan and studied there multiple times, and I do hope they can get their act together and fix this problem; it is a culture worth preserving.
